issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because the patient is the victim; a plausible trigger would be people resembling the perpetrator(s) or contextual robbery cues. As written, this item conflicts with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty/contaminated is not impossible after robbery, but in this profile it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise center on danger, self-blame, and moral injury rather than sexual violation or disgust-based trauma themes. This makes the appraisal set clinically inconsistent with the trauma context.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'Being naked' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless there was a stripping/sexual humiliation element, which is not suggested elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items point to perpetrator proximity and assault cues, making this vulnerability trigger clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally troubling behaviour during the event, but the rest of the profile reflects victim-focused danger, self-blame, and mistrust rather than any specific morally injurious action. In a mugging/robbery context this item is difficult to justify without corroborating memory/appraisal content about the patient's own behaviour.

vignette: Kaitlyn, a 35-year-old Pacific Islander woman married to her high school sweetheart, has found herself struggling with an intense sense of unease since being mugged on her way home from work three months ago. As an accountant living in the heart of a bustling city, Kaitlyn had grown accustomed to walking alone at night, feeling safe due to her routine and familiar surroundings. The traumatic event unfolded one evening as she was returning home after a long day at work. Lost in thought, planning for an upcoming meeting with clients, she heard footsteps behind her. Initially dismissing the sound, assuming it was just another pedestrian, Kaitlyn's heart began to race as the footsteps grew louder and more insistent. Before she could react fully, a man emerged from the shadows and demanded her purse. In a panic, Kaitlyn tried to keep hold of it but was jolted when he yanked it away, knocking her backward onto the pavement. The taste of asphalt lingered in her mouth as she lay there, dazed and disoriented. Since that night, Kaitlyn has found herself constantly on edge. The sound of footsteps near or behind her triggers vivid memories of the mugging. She can almost feel the jolt from when the offender pulled her purse away. When she hears any unexpected noise, it feels as though she is right back in that moment, tasting the pavement and feeling the rough ground beneath her. The experience has left Kaitlyn with a deep sense of distrust towards others and her surroundings. She often finds herself unable to relax even when she knows she is safe at home or at work. Her husband notices her hypervigilance and how she flinches at every sound, but no amount of reassurance from him can quell the fear that something bad might happen again. Kaitlyn's avoidance behaviors have become more pronounced over time. She avoids walking alone at night and has stopped going to social events where there are large crowds or unfamiliar environments. This has led to a growing sense of isolation as she misses out on spending time with friends and family. At work, her concentration is often disrupted by the memory of the event, particularly when she hears footsteps in the office hallway. The memory itself feels surreal and vivid at the same time. When it returns, Kaitlyn can taste the asphalt again and feel the rough ground beneath her, as if reliving every moment of the traumatic experience. She has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place and that she herself is somehow responsible for what happened due to some inherent flaw in her character. Her self-blame manifests in relentless rumination about what she could have done differently to prevent the mugging. Kaitlyn often isolates herself from others, deliberately trying to dissociate or blank out when memories overwhelm her. These strategies provide temporary relief but leave her feeling more isolated and disconnected from reality. What frightens Kaitlyn most is the constant fear that something bad will happen again, even in seemingly safe situations. The event has left her convinced that she can never fully trust her own safety or the reassurances of others. She dreads the idea of another unexpected touch or sound, knowing it might trigger a full-blown panic. Despite these struggles, Kaitlyn finally decided to seek help because the anxiety and avoidance were taking over her life. Her isolation has strained her relationships with friends and family, and her concentration at work is frequently disrupted by intrusive memories and hypervigilance. She hopes that with therapy, she can regain some sense of control and trust in herself and others again. Her primary fear is not being able to function normally in daily life and losing her job or relationships due to her condition. Kaitlyn's journey into therapy marks a crucial step towards reclaiming her peace of mind and re-engaging with the world around her, despite the lingering shadows cast by that fateful night.
